slides.text: You have built slices by hand. The standard library has a package, `slices`, with ready-made functions for the jobs you keep repeating: sorting, comparing and copying.

Three sessions:

- **1:** the basics of `slices`
- **2:** sorting by your own rule
- **3:** ties and order

A package is used by its name, a dot and a function, like `fmt.Println`. The `slices` functions take the slice as their first argument, so you do not write loops for common jobs.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
sort the list
is "go" in the list?
where is "go" in the list?
make a copy of the list

slides.text: Some functions change the slice they receive, like the one that sorts. Others only read it, and a few give back a new slice. Check which one you are calling before you rely on the old values.

exercises.title: Sort a slice
exercises.guide: Put the values of a slice in order.

chunks.guide: Import `slices` next to `fmt`. It holds ready-made functions for slices.

notes.text: Sorting, searching and more for slices.

chunks.guide: `slices.Sort` orders the slice in place, from smallest to largest. It returns nothing.
Text sorts too, in alphabetical order.

exercises.title: Search a slice
exercises.guide: Ask a slice if it holds a value, and where.

chunks.guide: A slice of tags.
`slices.Contains` answers with a bool.
`slices.Index` gives the position of the first match, or -1 when the value is not there.

notes.text: Not in the slice, so the answer is -1.

chunks.guide: `slices.Max` and `slices.Min` find the largest and the smallest value.

exercises.title: Find an id
exercises.guide: Print whether `ids` holds 3, then the position of 9.

exercises.title: Compare and copy
exercises.guide: Copy a slice, compare it, and change only the copy.

chunks.guide: `slices.Clone` makes a new slice with the same values. It shares nothing with the original.
Slices cannot be compared with `==`. `slices.Equal` compares length and values.
`slices.Reverse` flips a slice in place. Only the copy changes.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: Only the clone is sorted, so `nums` keeps its order. In the sorted slice, 5 sits at index 1.

slides.text:
`slices.Sort` goes from the smallest to the largest, and that is all it knows. For any other order, you give `slices.SortFunc` a rule: a function that compares two items, `a` and `b`, and answers with a number.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
rule(a, b):
    a goes first  -> a negative number
    a and b tie   -> 0
    b goes first  -> a positive number

slides.text:
The `cmp` package has `cmp.Compare(x, y)`, which gives exactly those answers for numbers and text. Swap its arguments and the order flips.

The rule is a function value, so it can be written in place or kept in a variable, as in the functions course.

exercises.title: Compare two values
exercises.guide: Ask `cmp.Compare` which of two values is bigger.

chunks.guide: `cmp.Compare` answers -1 when the first value is smaller, 0 when they are equal and 1 when it is bigger. The imports are already in the file.
Text is compared too, in alphabetical order.

exercises.title: Sort from the biggest
exercises.guide: Give `SortFunc` a rule that puts the biggest value first.

chunks.guide: A slice to sort. The imports are already in the file.
`slices.SortFunc` takes the slice and a rule. Swapping `a` and `b` in `cmp.Compare` reverses the order.

notes.text: Reversed, so bigger values go first.

chunks.guide: The same rule works for text: the last word in the alphabet comes first.

exercises.title: Highest score first
exercises.guide: Sort `scores` from the highest to the lowest.

exercises.title: Sort by length
exercises.guide: Sort words by how long they are, not by their letters.

chunks.guide: Four words of different lengths. The imports are already in the file.
A rule can live in a variable. This one compares the lengths of the words.
Pass the rule to `SortFunc` by its name.
Swap the arguments to put the longest word first.

output.text:
[fig kiwi apple banana]
[banana apple kiwi fig]

exercises.title: What is it for?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick what it is for.
options: Drops the names that share a length
exercises.explanation: The arguments are swapped, so a longer `b` makes the answer positive and moves it before `a`: the longest names come first.

slides.text: Two items that compare equal are a tie. `SortFunc` may leave tied items in any order, so a result with ties can change from one Go version to another. `SortStableFunc` keeps them in the order they already had.

To break a tie yourself, compare by one thing and then by another. `cmp.Or` returns the first answer that is not zero, so it does exactly that.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
compare the lengths
if they tie, compare the letters
if they still tie, they are equal

exercises.title: Break a tie
exercises.guide: Sort by length, and by letters when two words tie.

chunks.guide: Words that share a length: a tie to break. The imports are already in the file.
`cmp.Or` returns the first of its arguments that is not 0. The letters only matter when the lengths tie.

notes.text: Takes the first answer that is not 0.

exercises.title: Keep the original order
exercises.guide: Sort by length without moving words that tie.

chunks.guide: Three words of 2 letters and two of 3. The imports are already in the file.
`SortStableFunc` keeps tied items in their original order, so `al`, `cy` and `jo` stay in that order.

notes.text: Equal items keep the order they had.

exercises.title: Stable by length
What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: The words sort by length: `go`, `fig`, then the three 4-letter words. A stable sort keeps `pear`, `kiwi`, `plum` in their original order.

exercises.title: Is it sorted?
exercises.guide: Ask whether a slice is in order, before and after sorting.

chunks.guide: An unsorted slice. The imports are already in the file.
`IsSorted` is true once the slice goes from smallest to largest.
A slice sorted from the biggest is not sorted for `IsSorted`.
